strengths: The core idea of avoiding iterative reconstruction by directly inverting to the diffusion latent via a short PF-ODE trajectory and scoring typicality is a novel and interesting reframing of diffusion-based anomaly detection, distinct from the reconstruction-error paradigm used by prior work.

Table 1 provides a genuinely useful systematic comparison of prior diffusion-based AD methods along axes such as synthetic-anomaly usage, NFE, timestep tuning, sampler type, and scoring function, clarifying the design space.

The method achieves large inference speedups (2-64x) relative to competing diffusion-based approaches while remaining broadly competitive on MVTecAD, which is a meaningful practical contribution for real-time deployment scenarios.

The ablation in Sec 5.3/5.4 comparing reconstruction-based vs. inversion-based scoring across step counts, and the discovery of the 'reverse-scoring' phenomenon with pure NLL, is a genuinely informative empirical finding connecting to known issues in flow-based OOD detection.
Incorporating a pretrained backbone into a feature-space diffusion model is a reasonable and apparently effective design choice that meaningfully improves results over raw pixel-space diffusion.
weaknesses: There is a substantial mismatch between the paper's central claimed contribution ('direct latent likelihood evaluation', title, abstract, and Table 1 which lists 'log pθ(xT)' as the anomaly score) and the actual best-performing method used in experiments (Algorithm 1 and Sec 4.4), which is a heuristic spatial-norm difference score, not a likelihood. Section 5.4 explicitly shows the pure NLL score fails and is unreliable, undermining the paper's own framing and central theoretical motivation.

The abstract's headline number (AUC 0.991 at 15 FPS) appears to conflate two different configurations: 'Ours' achieves 64ms/~15FPS latency but only 97.3/93.7 AUC, while 'Ours*' achieves 99.1/94.8 AUC but at 85ms (~11.8 FPS) latency with per-category step tuning. Presenting these as a single combined achievement in the abstract is misleading.

Performance on VisA is considerably weaker than competing methods for the default 'Ours' configuration (79.1 image-level AUC vs. 98-99% for prior methods), and even the tuned 'Ours*' variant trails most baselines noticeably in several categories (e.g., capsules, macaroni2, pcb2), raising concerns about generalization beyond MVTecAD.

The theoretical justification for omitting the Jacobian term in the change-of-variables likelihood is thin; the paper appeals to analogy with normalizing-flow AD methods but does not analyze the error introduced by both the Jacobian omission and the very coarse Euler discretization (2-5 steps), which likely dominates any theoretical approximation error.

'Ours*' requires per-category tuning of S over {2,3,4,5} using presumably held-out performance, which risks implicitly using test/validation anomaly information despite the paper's stated goal of avoiding hyperparameter tuning that exploits anomaly information — a criticism the paper itself levels at competing methods.

Reproducibility details are limited: architectural specifics of the UNet diffusion model, feature-space dimensions per dataset, and exact backbone layer choices are not fully specified, and no code availability is mentioned.

Some entries in Tables 1-3 are missing (e.g., latency for DiffAD/ScoreDD, pixel-level AUC for several VisA baselines), limiting the completeness of the comparison the paper relies on to support its speed-accuracy trade-off claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important practical problem – the high latency of reconstruction-based diffusion anomaly detectors – and proposes a conceptually elegant reformulation (image → latent inversion via PF-ODE, with anomaly scoring on the latent side) that avoids per-image reconstruction and eliminates the need to tune a noise-injection timestep, which is a real pain point of prior diffusion-AD methods.

Substantial and well-demonstrated speed advantage: 64–85 ms latency vs. 617–4140 ms for competing diffusion-based methods (Table 2/3), which is a meaningful systems-level contribution even where accuracy is close.

The ablation in Sec. 5.3/5.4 comparing reconstruction-based vs. inversion-based scoring across different S and perturbation percentages is informative and honestly reports a failure mode (the 'reverse-scoring' problem with naive NLL) rather than hiding it, and the paper analyzes it with a histogram visualization (Fig. 2).

The feature-space diffusion model (training the diffusion process on frozen pretrained backbone features rather than raw pixels) is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated design choice that plausibly explains the competitive MVTecAD numbers despite very few NFEs.

Table 1 gives a clear, useful qualitative comparison of design choices (NFE, timestep tuning, use of synthetic anomalies, sampler, scoring function) across many prior diffusion-AD papers, situating the contribution well within the literature.
weaknesses: The core theoretical motivation of the method – evaluating the Gaussian prior log-likelihood of the inverted latent – is shown empirically to fail (the 'reverse-scoring problem'), and the paper falls back to an ad hoc spatial-norm heuristic (Eq. 17) with no rigorous justification; this is a significant gap between the stated contribution ("directly infer latent variables and measure density under the Gaussian prior") and what is actually used to obtain the reported numbers, and the explanation offered (analogy to flow-based OOD literature) is not developed into a real theoretical account, only flagged as future work.

Performance on VisA is substantially weaker than competing methods: the default configuration (S=2) achieves only 79.1% average image-level AUC vs. 98.5–99.5% for prior diffusion-based methods, and even the tuned variant (Ours*, S∈{2..5}) reaches only 95.8% vs. up to 99.5%, with some categories (e.g., capsules 58.3%, macaroni2 47.9% for S=2) showing very poor detection – this is a serious limitation that is understated in the text, which frames the gap merely as "a performance gap remains."

There is an internal inconsistency between the abstract's headline claim ("AUC of 0.991 at 15 FPS") and Table 2: the 99.1% AUC corresponds to "Ours*" at 85 ms (≈11.8 FPS), while 15 FPS (64 ms) corresponds to "Ours" (S=2) at only 97.3% AUC; conflating these two configurations in the abstract is misleading and should be corrected.

Pixel-level localization AUC on MVTecAD (93.7% / 94.8%) is noticeably lower than most compared methods (96.7–98.7%), and no qualitative segmentation maps are shown to assess where/why the spatial-norm-based localization underperforms, despite localization being emphasized as a use case in Sec. 4.4.

The claimed omission of the Jacobian term (Eq. 16) is discussed conceptually and promised as an experimental question ("we conduct experiments to evaluate the impact of the Jacobian"), but no explicit ablation numerically comparing with-Jacobian vs. without-Jacobian performance is presented in the manuscript, leaving this claim unsubstantiated.

Evaluation is limited to two industrial benchmarks (MVTecAD, VisA); there is no analysis of variance across seeds/runs, no wall-clock breakdown by hardware, and no code/artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility assessment.

The write-up contains duplicated/redundant paragraphs (e.g., the end of Sec. 3.4 and the middle of Sec. 4.3 each repeat nearly identical text blocks), suggesting insufficient proofreading; while not a technical flaw, it affects clarity and polish.

strengths: Proposes a conceptually clean and well-motivated reformulation of diffusion-based anomaly detection: instead of the conventional noise-then-denoise reconstruction paradigm, the method performs DDIM/PF-ODE inversion in a learned feature (latent) space and scores anomalies via deviation from the tractable Gaussian prior, eliminating explicit reconstruction and its associated noise-strength tuning sensitivity.

Strong efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated: the method achieves substantially higher FPS (e.g., 88.1 on MVTecAD) than all compared diffusion-based baselines while maintaining state-of-the-art or highly competitive AU-ROC/AP/F1/AU-PRO across MVTecAD, VisA, and MPDD in both multi-class and single-class settings.

The paper includes a thorough set of ablations: sensitivity of reconstruction-based methods to noise ratio/diffusion steps (Table 4) versus robustness of the inversion approach, backbone choice (Table 6), diffusion architecture choice (Table 7), and scoring scheme (NLL vs Abs vs combined, Appendix Table 13), which meaningfully support the paper's core claims about robustness and design choices.

Demonstrates plug-and-play generalizability by inserting the inference-stage InvAD scheme into existing diffusion-based AD models (DeCoDiff, MDM), showing efficiency and/or accuracy gains, and additionally evaluates on a medical imaging benchmark (BMAD) showing state-of-the-art results with large efficiency improvement, suggesting the approach is not narrowly tailored to one domain.
The derivation connecting DDIM sampling/inversion to the PF-ODE and the appendix providing detailed proofs, hyperparameters, and dataset statistics support reproducibility and technical transparency.
weaknesses: The core anomaly scoring mechanism (deviation from prior distribution via NLL/Abs on the normalized latent) is a fairly direct application of known inversion/typicality ideas (e.g., ScoreDD, Heng et al. 2024 OOD detection) to the AD setting; the novelty is more in problem reformulation and efficient combination than in a fundamentally new technique, which somewhat limits originality.

The pixel-level localization performance (AU-ROC, AP, F1_max, AU-PRO) is often only middling relative to top baselines (e.g., Table 2 shows InvAD frequently below OmiAD/HVQ-Trans on pixel-level AP and F1_max), indicating the efficiency-accuracy trade-off is not uniformly favorable for localization, despite strong image-level detection numbers.

The theoretical claim that anomalous latents fall into 'low-density regions' under PF-ODE is asserted rather than rigorously proven or empirically validated (e.g., no direct visualization or quantitative analysis of the latent distribution/typicality gap between normal and anomalous samples beyond downstream AUROC numbers), leaving the central mechanism somewhat under-justified.

The reverse-scoring problem motivating the switch from pure NLL to the NLL+Abs combination is only briefly mentioned with a pointer to supplementary material, but the supplementary material does not provide a deep quantitative characterization of when/why this problem occurs, limiting the completeness of this justification.

Reliance on a fixed small step subset (S=3) with heuristically chosen timesteps (e.g., {333,666,999}) appears somewhat ad hoc; while shown empirically robust across S in Table 4, no principled explanation for how these specific timesteps were chosen is provided, and generalization of this choice to substantially different datasets/domains is not deeply analyzed.

Some comparisons (e.g., single-class Table 3/11) omit certain pixel-level metrics (AP, F1_max) that are reported in the multi-class tables, making it harder to fully assess localization quality consistency across settings.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated paradigm shift from reconstruction-based to inversion-based (reconstruction-free) diffusion AD, with a coherent theoretical narrative connecting PF-ODE inversion, DDIM, and prior-distribution typicality scoring (including a full derivation of the DDIM inversion update in the appendix).

Strong efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated: the method attains 88.1 FPS versus <40 FPS for all compared diffusion-based baselines in Table 1/2, while matching or exceeding their image-level AU-ROC/AP on MVTecAD, VisA, and MPDD under both multi-class and single-class settings.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation: multi-class (Table 2) and single-class (Table 3, Table 11) industrial benchmarks, a medical-imaging benchmark (BMAD, Appendix D/Table 12), and a plug-and-play generalizability study where InvAD is inserted into DeCoDiff and MDM (Table 5), showing consistent inference-time gains.

Careful ablations covering the effect of noise-strength/step-count sensitivity versus a conventional reconstruction-based baseline (Table 4), backbone feature-space choice (Table 6), diffusion architecture (Table 7), and the anomaly-scoring formula (Appendix Table 13), which together substantiate the design choices rather than merely reporting a single configuration.

Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, dataset statistics, hardware/software environment, and fixed seeds are reported in the appendix, and the method is framed as an inference-only, architecture-agnostic module that can be added to existing diffusion AD pipelines.
weaknesses: The core mechanism (typicality/likelihood of an inverted latent under a known prior as an anomaly indicator) is conceptually close to established OOD/typicality-testing ideas (e.g., Nalisnick et al. 2019, Osada et al. 2023, cited in the paper) and to existing score/latent-space diffusion AD baselines (ScoreDD, DDAD); the paper would benefit from a more precise articulation of what is fundamentally new beyond combining PF-ODE inversion with a heuristic NLL+Abs scoring rule.

Pixel-level localization results are not uniformly state-of-the-art: on MVTecAD (Table 2) InvAD's pixel AU-ROC (97.5) and F1_max (52.3) trail OmiAD (97.7, 56.7), and qualitative maps in Figures 2-4 are sometimes visibly more diffuse/noisy than competitors (e.g., pill, screw, capsule categories), which somewhat undercuts the claim of "comparable" localization quality.

The anomaly-scoring scheme (NLL + Abs) is justified mainly empirically (Table 13) rather than derived theoretically; the paper acknowledges the reverse-scoring problem but the combination rule feels ad hoc and its generality across datasets/backbones is not deeply analyzed.

When integrated into existing diffusion AD models as a plug-and-play module (Table 5), accuracy actually drops for DeCoDiff (-2.0/-2.8 AU-ROC) despite FPS gains; this accuracy-efficiency trade-off in the generalizability setting is not explicitly discussed as a limitation, which slightly overstates the "model-agnostic" benefit.

The method still requires multiple NFEs (S=3) rather than a single step, and the paper explicitly defers single-step distillation to future work, so the "reconstruction-free"/"tuning-free" efficiency claims are somewhat qualified rather than fully realized.

Results appear to be from single runs without variance/confidence intervals across seeds, which is common in this literature but limits statistical confidence in the reported margins, several of which are narrow (e.g., mAD differences of <1 point versus the second-best method in some tables).
